headline: The AG-prosecutor split returns after eight years. Who confirms the new prosecutor stays unsettled.
context: On 18 May 2026 the parliamentary committee chaired by Azalina Othman Said held its sixth meeting on the bill to separate the Attorney-General and Public Prosecutor, fused in one office since 1957. She called it 'the best compromise'. The report is not public.

cards.big: Malaysia will split the Attorney-General and Public Prosecutor for the first time since 1957. Splitting the office is the easy part; deciding who confirms the new prosecutor is not.
cards.sub: The 2018 Pakatan Harapan manifesto promised to separate them 'immediately'. Eight years and four AGs later, Azalina calls it 'the best compromise'. The bill returns 22 June.

cards.big: Article 145 has placed prosecution and the government's legal advice in one executive-appointed officer since 1957. The bill finally separates the two.
cards.sub: Article 145(1) puts the Attorney-General's appointment with the Yang di-Pertuan Agong on the Prime Minister's advice. Article 145(3) gives that one officer discretion to start or drop criminal cases.

cards.big: Ten government MPs led by Rafizi Ramli demanded a Dewan Rakyat vote to confirm the new prosecutor. None were named to the committee that shaped the compromise.
cards.sub: On 24 February 2026 the ten PKR backbenchers asked for a public confirmation hearing and a parliamentary vote before any nominee reaches the Agong. The committee seated other MPs.

cards.big: The new prosecutor would be recommended by the Judicial and Legal Service Commission, the body the Attorney-General sits on. As tabled, the bill added no parliamentary vote.
cards.sub: Attorney-General Dusuki says the bill gives the Prime Minister no role in choosing the prosecutor. The Bar Council's reply: the AG's seat on that commission keeps executive influence in the room.

cards.big: Separation is not independence. The office split has consensus; the vote to let Parliament confirm the prosecutor does not, and its backers were kept off the committee.
Picture giving the umpire his own office, then still choosing him through a panel the team captain sits on, with no open vote on the pick.
cards.sub: The bill creates a standalone prosecutor. The commission that recommends the prosecutor still includes the Attorney-General.

cards.big: Eight years to agree on splitting the office. Deciding who confirms the new prosecutor fell to a committee that left out the MPs who demanded a say.
